title: Lowest Point on the Trail
story: A hiking app records your route as a list of waypoint altitudes. Walking forward adds a waypoint. Retracing your steps from a dead end drops the waypoints you walk back over, so the list is always your path from the trailhead.
The screen shows your current altitude and the lowest altitude on your current path, refreshed after every step, so both values must be available instantly, even with thousands of waypoints.
task:
• step(altitude) adds a waypoint at the end of the path.
  • back() removes the most recent waypoint.
  • current() returns the altitude of the most recent waypoint.
  • lowest() returns the lowest altitude among all waypoints still on the path.
Every method must run in O(1) time.
constraints: -1,000 ≤ altitude ≤ 10,000 (metres; negative means below sea level). Altitudes may repeat.
back, current and lowest are only called when the path has at least one waypoint.

examples.explanation: The hiker walks to 340 m, 280 m and then 410 m, so the lowest altitude is 280. Backing off 410 does not change the lowest, but backing off 280 as well leaves only 340, so both lowest and current return 340.

hints: Suppose you walk to 500 and then to 200, so the lowest is 200, and then you back off 200. If you stored only one variable low = 200, how would you know the new lowest is 500?
After the lowest waypoint is removed, the answer is the lowest the path had before that waypoint was added. That value must still be stored somewhere.
The path only changes at its end, so it behaves like a stack. What if every entry also remembered the lowest altitude up to and including itself?
Push pairs (altitude, lowestSoFar), where lowestSoFar = min(altitude, lowestSoFar of the entry below). back pops a pair, current reads the top altitude, lowest reads the top's lowestSoFar.
bruteForce: Keep altitudes in an array and scan it on every lowest() call. That is O(n) per call and O(n²) over a hike of n waypoints.
A single low variable is fast but wrong: it cannot recover the previous low after back() removes the lowest waypoint.

tests.note: the lowest point is retraced: a single min variable goes stale
equal lows: one copy is retraced, the other is still on the path
climbing: the start stays the lowest
descending: each back raises the lowest
path retraced to the start, then a new step

js: this.path = []; // entries: [altitude, lowest altitude up to here]
py: self.path = []  # entries: (altitude, lowest altitude up to here)
below = self.path[-1][1] if self.path else altitude
walkthrough: The path changes only at its end, so it is a stack. The hard part is lowest() after a back(). To solve it, store with each waypoint the lowest altitude of the path at that moment. Popping then restores the old answer, because the entry below still holds it.
• step 340 has no entry below it, so push (340, 340).
• step 410 gives min(410, 280) = 280, so push (410, 280). lowest() reads the top entry and returns 280.
• The two back calls pop (410, 280) and then (280, 280), so the top is now (340, 340).
solution.timeWhy: Every method does one push, one pop, or one read at the top of the stack.
solution.spaceWhy: Two numbers per waypoint on the path.
solution.takeaway: To answer a question about a whole stack in O(1), store the answer for each prefix with the entry that ends it. Popping rolls the answer back automatically. The same trick gives an O(1) maximum, sum or count.
